name: Capellini
look: Very thin round strands, under a millimetre across.
fact: Its name means little hairs, which is exactly how delicate it is; it suits light sauces and broths that will not weigh it down.

name: Capellini d'angelo
look: The finest of the dried strands, usually sold coiled into small nests.
fact: Even thinner than capellini, angel hair can overcook in well under two minutes, which is why it is often simply dropped into hot broth.

name: Fedelini
look: Thin round strands, between capellini and spaghettini in thickness.
fact: A very old Ligurian shape: Genoa's pasta makers were organised as a guild of "fidelari" with written statutes in 1574.

name: Spaghettini
look: Round strands a little thinner than standard spaghetti.
fact: It cooks a couple of minutes faster than spaghetti, so a distracted minute can ruin it; cooks favour it for oil-based and seafood sauces.

name: Maccheroncini di Campofilone
look: Hair-thin golden egg strands, cut very fine and dried in flat skeins.
fact: A protected (IGP) pasta from one village in the Marche, made with only eggs and flour, no water. It is cut so fine that it cooks in a minute or two.

name: Sōmen
look: Very thin, white wheat strands, under 1.3 mm across.
fact: The dough is stretched, not cut, with a film of oil to keep it from drying. In summer it is served cold, sometimes sent down a bamboo flume of running water (nagashi-sōmen).

name: Misua
look: Hair-thin, salted wheat strands that turn very soft when cooked.
fact: From Fujian, the dough is pulled by hand into threads and hung to dry. It is a birthday and festival food because the long strands stand for long life.

name: Rice vermicelli
look: Thin, white, round rice strands, usually sold dried in brittle bundles.
fact: Made by extruding rice paste into hot water, it needs only a brief soak. It is the base noodle of much of southern China and Southeast Asia.

name: Cellophane noodles
look: Wiry, thin starch strands that turn clear and slippery when cooked.
fact: Made from mung bean starch rather than grain flour, which is why they turn transparent. Longkou in Shandong has been the famous production centre for centuries.

name: Naengmyeon
look: Thin, very chewy grey-brown strands made from buckwheat and starch.
fact: A northern Korean speciality, associated with Pyongyang and Hamhung, that spread south after the Korean War. The strands are so elastic that they are often cut with scissors at the table.

name: Idiyappam
look: Lacy little nests of very fine steamed rice strands.
fact: Rice-flour dough is squeezed through a perforated press into tangled discs and steamed, not boiled. It is a breakfast staple in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka.

name: Seviyan
look: Very fine wheat vermicelli, usually broken short and often sold pre-roasted.
fact: Usually toasted in ghee before cooking, which keeps the strands separate. Simmered in sweet milk with dates and nuts it becomes sheer khurma, a classic Eid dish.

name: Khanom chin
look: Thin, soft, white rice strands served fresh, folded into small skeins.
fact: The rice is traditionally fermented for a few days before being made into dough and pressed through a sieve into boiling water. The name is thought to come from the Mon language.

name: Wonton noodles
look: Thin, yellow, springy egg noodles.
fact: A Cantonese alkaline egg noodle. The dough was traditionally kneaded by a cook bouncing on a long bamboo pole, a craft that is now rare.

name: Spaghetti
look: Long, round, solid strands about 2 mm across.
fact: Its name means little strings, from spago, twine. The word only became common in the 1800s; earlier the shape was simply called vermicelli or maccheroni.

name: Vermicelli
look: Long round strands, a touch thicker than spaghetti in Italy.
fact: In Italy it is slightly thicker than spaghetti, the opposite of export labels, where the name marks a thinner strand. It is the old Neapolitan name for the shape.

name: Spaghetti alla chitarra
look: Fresh egg strands with a square cross-section and a porous surface.
fact: A sheet of dough is pressed with a rolling pin through a wooden frame strung with steel wires, the chitarra. Each strand comes out square, not round, and rough enough to hold sauce.

name: Tonnarelli
look: Fresh egg strands with a square section, slightly thicker than spaghetti.
fact: The Roman name for chitarra-style square spaghetti. Its rough, starchy surface helps pecorino and pepper emulsify, so many Roman trattorie prefer it for cacio e pepe.

name: Soba
look: Thin, grey-brown buckwheat noodles with a squared-off section.
fact: Buckwheat has no gluten, so most soba includes some wheat flour to hold together. Toshikoshi soba is eaten on New Year's Eve; the easily cut strands stand for letting go of the old year.

name: Hiyamugi
look: Thin white wheat strands, between sōmen and udon in thickness.
fact: Japanese standards separate dried wheat noodles by width: under 1.3 mm is sōmen, 1.3 to 1.7 mm is hiyamugi, thicker is udon. Bundles sometimes include a few pink or green strands.

name: Ramen
look: Yellowish, springy wheat strands, straight or wavy.
fact: The dough is made with kansui, an alkaline mineral water that gives the yellow tint and firm, bouncy chew. Both the noodle and its name came to Japan from China.

name: Lo mein noodles
look: Round, yellow wheat-and-egg noodles about as thick as spaghetti.
fact: The same noodle serves two dishes: lo mein is boiled and tossed with sauce, while chow mein ("fried noodles") is stir-fried or crisped in the wok.

name: Yi mein
look: Golden, spongy egg noodles sold as large dried cakes.
fact: The noodles are deep-fried before drying, which gives them a spongy, chewy bite. Served uncut at birthdays and banquets, where the long strands stand for long life.

name: Pancit canton
look: Round, yellow wheat-and-egg noodles, usually sold dried in tangled blocks.
fact: Brought by Chinese traders and now thoroughly Filipino. Pancit is a fixture at birthday tables, where long noodles stand for long life.

name: Dangmyeon
look: Long, greyish, translucent strands, thicker and chewier than other glass noodles.
fact: Made from sweet potato starch, the noodles turn glassy and springy when boiled. They are the base of japchae, stir-fried with vegetables and sesame oil.

name: Mixian
look: Round, smooth, white rice noodles about as thick as spaghetti.
fact: The everyday noodle of Yunnan. In "crossing-the-bridge" noodles it is slipped at the table into a bowl of broth kept scalding under a layer of fat.

name: Spaghettoni
look: Round strands noticeably thicker than spaghetti.
fact: It is thicker than spaghetti, so it takes longer to cook and keeps more bite, standing up to robust, oily and peppery sauces.

name: Bigoli
look: Thick, long strands with a rough, porous surface.
fact: A thick, solid strand from the Veneto, pressed through a hand-cranked press called a bigolaro, often with whole-wheat flour or duck eggs. Bigoli in salsa was the classic dish for meatless days.

name: Troccoli
look: Thick fresh strands with a squarish to oval section.
fact: Typical of Foggia and nearby Basilicata. The strands are cut by rolling a grooved pin, the troccolaturo, over a thick sheet of dough.

name: Strangozzi
look: Thick, eggless strands with a rectangular section, hand-cut from a sheet.
fact: The name recalls leather shoelaces. Legend says rebels in the Papal States used such laces to strangle priests, hence the link with strozzapreti.

name: Udon
look: Thick, white, soft and chewy wheat noodles.
fact: Made from just flour, salt and water. The stiff dough was traditionally kneaded underfoot; Sanuki udon from Kagawa is the most famous regional style.

name: Hokkien noodles
look: Thick, round, yellow wheat noodles, sold fresh and lightly oiled.
fact: Introduced by migrants from Fujian (Hokkien) province in China. Alkaline water gives the yellow colour and a chew that stands up to fierce wok heat.

name: Bánh canh
look: Thick, short-ish, slippery white noodles, similar in size to udon.
fact: Made from tapioca flour, rice flour or a blend, which makes the noodles chewy and slightly translucent. Their starch helps thicken the broth.

name: Bucatini
look: Thick spaghetti-like strands with a narrow hole down the centre.
fact: The name comes from buco, hole. The channel lets water in so the thick strand cooks evenly, and it draws sauce inside as well as outside.

name: Perciatelli
look: Long hollow strands, typically a little thicker than bucatini.
fact: The Neapolitan name for bucatini-style pasta, from perciare, to pierce. In southern Italy it is often treated as the rustic cousin of bucatini.

name: Ziti lunghi
look: Long, smooth, hollow tubes about 25 cm long and wider than bucatini.
fact: Zita means bride in southern dialects, and this was the pasta of wedding feasts. Traditionally it is snapped into pieces by hand before cooking.

name: Candele
look: Very long, smooth, wide tubes, thicker than ziti.
fact: Named for the long candles carried in religious processions. Like ziti, it is broken by hand into uneven lengths that catch thick Neapolitan sauces.

name: Fusilli lunghi
look: Spaghetti-length solid strand wound into a springy coil, like an old telephone cord.
fact: The shape descends from handmade fusilli, made by winding a strand of dough around a thin iron rod and sliding it off.

name: Pici
look: Fat, uneven, hand-rolled strands like very thick spaghetti.
fact: From the Siena area, each strand is rolled by hand from flour and water into an uneven rope. No two are identical, and that irregularity is considered the point.

name: Umbricelli
look: Thick, irregular hand-rolled strands of flour and water.
fact: Umbria's answer to Tuscan pici. The name comes from the dialect word for earthworm, a frank description of the hand-rolled shape.

name: Maccheroni alla mugnaia
look: One very long, thick, uneven rope of pasta gathered into a skein.
fact: A speciality of Elice in the province of Pescara. A ring of dough is worked by hand, stretched and doubled over and over, until it becomes a single continuous strand.

name: Lamian
look: Long, smooth wheat strands, pulled to any thickness from hair-thin to chopstick-thick.
fact: The cook stretches and folds a rope of dough, doubling the number of strands with each pull. Lanzhou beef noodle soup is its best-known home.

name: Laghman
look: Thick, chewy, hand-pulled wheat noodles.
fact: A dish of the Uyghurs that spread across Central Asia; its name derives from Chinese lamian. The oiled dough is pulled into long strands by hand, then topped with a meat and vegetable stew.

name: Linguine
look: Long strands flattened into a narrow oval, about 3 mm wide.
fact: Its name means little tongues. The flattened, lens-shaped section sits between round spaghetti and a true flat ribbon.

name: Linguettine
look: A slimmer, more delicate version of linguine.
fact: This slimmer linguine variant cooks quickly and is prized for lighter seafood sauces.

name: Bavette
look: Narrow flattened strands with a slightly convex section, a little wider than linguine.
fact: One of the old shapes of Genoa. Some pasta makers treat bavette and linguine as the same thing; others make bavette slightly wider and flatter.

name: Trenette
look: Narrow, fairly thick ribbons, similar to linguine.
fact: In Liguria the classic pesto plate is trenette with potatoes and green beans boiled in the same pot and mixed in, not served as sides.
pairings: pesto with potatoes and green beans

name: Tagliolini
look: Very narrow, thin egg ribbons, 2 to 3 mm wide.
fact: Essentially a much finer cousin of tagliatelle, cut from the same egg sheet. It cooks in a minute or two and is often served in broth.

name: Tajarin
look: Very thin, narrow ribbons of deep yellow egg dough.
fact: The Piedmontese tagliolini, made with an unusually yolk-rich dough; traditional recipes from the Langhe call for 30 or more yolks per kilo of flour.

name: Paglia e fieno
look: A mix of yellow egg ribbons and green spinach ribbons, sold in nests.
fact: The plain egg strands are the straw and the spinach-tinted ones the hay. The two are cooked and served together.

name: Fieno di Canepina
look: Extremely thin, narrow egg ribbons, as fine as angel hair.
fact: A traditional product of Canepina, near Viterbo. The ribbons are cut so fine by hand that they are compared to hay.

name: Pillus
look: Thin, narrow, fresh egg ribbons.
fact: A Sardinian fresh pasta. In Busachi it is cooked in mutton broth with saffron and fresh sheep's cheese for the festive dish su succu.

name: Bánh phở
look: Flat, white, soft rice ribbons, a few millimetres wide.
fact: A thin rice batter is steamed into sheets and then sliced into ribbons. Sold fresh in Vietnam, and dried abroad as rice sticks.

name: Sen lek
look: Narrow, flat rice noodles about 3 mm wide.
fact: Thai rice noodles are named by width: sen mi is hair-thin, sen lek narrow and sen yai wide. Sen lek is the one used for pad thai.

name: Reshteh
look: Thin, flat, narrow wheat noodles, pale or toasted brown.
fact: Eaten around Nowruz, the Persian New Year, when the noodles are said to stand for the threads of life and taking hold of one's path for the year ahead.

name: Kal-guksu
look: Soft, flat, hand-cut wheat noodles.
fact: The dough is rolled thin, folded and sliced with a knife, not extruded or pulled. The noodles are boiled straight in the broth, which their starch thickens.

name: Tagliatelle
look: Long, thin egg ribbons about 7 to 8 mm wide.
fact: Bologna's Chamber of Commerce keeps a solid gold tagliatella, deposited in 1972, that fixes the ideal width at 8 mm once cooked.

name: Fettuccine
look: Long egg ribbons, about as wide as tagliatelle and usually a touch thicker.
fact: The Roman counterpart of tagliatelle. Fettuccine Alfredo began in Rome in the early 1900s, when restaurateur Alfredo Di Lelio tossed them with just butter and Parmigiano.

name: Fettuccelle
look: Flat dried semolina ribbons, a little narrower than fettuccine.
fact: A dried, eggless take on fettuccine made by southern pasta factories. It is firmer than the fresh egg ribbon and suits seafood and tomato sauces.

name: Bandnudeln
look: Flat egg noodle ribbons, usually sold dried in loose nests.
fact: Germany's everyday egg ribbon. It is usually served as a side dish to soak up gravy, not as a course of its own.

name: Lokshen
look: Flat egg noodles, cut fine for soup or wide for baking.
fact: The egg noodles of Ashkenazi Jewish cooking across Eastern Europe. Fine ones go into chicken soup, and wide ones are baked into kugel, sweet or savoury.

name: Metélt
look: Flat, hand-cut egg noodle ribbons.
fact: Hungarian cut noodles are as likely to be sweet as savoury: tossed with ground poppy seeds and sugar (mákos metélt) or with walnuts (diós metélt).

name: Kesme
look: Flat, hand-cut egg noodles.
fact: The name is simply the Turkic word for "cut". Egg dough is rolled out, dried briefly, sliced into strips and cooked in a meat broth.

name: Mee pok
look: Flat, yellow egg noodles of medium width.
fact: A noodle of Teochew origin. It is most often served "dry", meaning tossed with chili, vinegar and oil, with the soup on the side.

name: Pappardelle
look: Broad egg ribbons, 2 to 3 cm wide.
fact: Its name comes from the Tuscan verb pappare, to gobble up. The broad surface is built for rich game ragù.

name: Lasagnette
look: Wide ribbons, narrower than lasagne, with straight or wavy edges.
fact: A narrow lasagna meant to be tossed with sauce like a ribbon, not layered and baked.

name: Picagge
look: Wide, thin fresh ribbons, about 1.5 to 2 cm across.
fact: The name is Genoese dialect for cloth ribbons or tapes. Green picagge are coloured with borage or chard, and picagge matte include chestnut flour.

name: Lagane
look: Wide, short, fairly thick ribbons of eggless semolina dough.
fact: The name goes back to Latin laganum; the poet Horace wrote of going home to a bowl of leeks, chickpeas and lagana. Lagane with chickpeas is still eaten in Basilicata and Calabria.

name: Biangbiang noodles
look: Very wide, long, thick hand-pulled wheat ribbons, like a belt.
fact: From Shaanxi. The name is said to echo the slap of dough on the counter as it is stretched, and it is written with a character of more than 50 strokes missing from standard dictionaries.

name: Ho fun
look: Wide, flat, slippery white rice ribbons, sold fresh.
fact: Named after Shahe, now part of Guangzhou. Rice batter is steamed into thin sheets, oiled and cut; the same noodle became kway teow and sen yai in Southeast Asia.

name: Kishimen
look: Broad, thin, flat wheat noodles, like flattened udon.
fact: The signature noodle of Nagoya. Being thinner than udon it cooks faster and has a smooth, slippery texture.

name: Hōtō
look: Wide, flat, thick wheat noodles.
fact: A speciality of Yamanashi. The noodles are simmered raw in a miso stew with pumpkin, without being boiled first, so their starch thickens the broth.

name: Mì Quảng
look: Wide, flat rice noodles, often tinted yellow with turmeric.
fact: Named for Quảng Nam province in central Vietnam. It is served with only a shallow pool of concentrated broth, plus herbs, peanuts and a toasted rice cracker.

name: Kuanfen
look: Broad, translucent, very chewy starch ribbons.
fact: Made mostly from sweet potato starch, these wide glass noodles soak up broth and are a hot pot favourite in Sichuan and Chongqing.

name: Liangpi
look: Wide, slippery, translucent ribbons served cold.
fact: Wheat dough is rinsed in water to wash out the starch. The starchy water is left to settle, steamed into thin sheets and cut; the leftover gluten is served alongside.

name: Mafaldine
look: Long flat ribbons with ruffled edges on both sides.
fact: Named in honour of Princess Mafalda of Savoy, born in 1902. The alias reginette means little queens. The flat centre and thinner frills cook to two different textures.

name: Tripoline
look: Long ribbons ruffled along one edge only.
fact: Said to have been named to mark Italy's conquest of Tripoli, Libya, in 1911. The single frilled edge makes the ribbon curl as it cooks.

name: Pizzoccheri
look: Short, flat, grey-brown ribbons about 1 cm wide and 7 cm long.
fact: From Teglio in the Valtellina, made mostly of buckwheat flour with a little wheat. Traditionally boiled with cabbage and potato, then layered with Casera cheese and garlic butter.

name: Scialatielli
look: Short, thick, slightly irregular fresh ribbons.
fact: One of the few pastas with a known inventor: Amalfi chef Enrico Cosentino, who won a culinary prize with it in 1978. The dough includes milk, basil and grated cheese.

name: Sagne 'ncannulate
look: Long semolina ribbons twisted into loose spirals.
fact: From the Salento. Each strip is twisted by hand around itself and left to dry in a curl, so sauce collects in the folds.

name: Sagne
look: Short, uneven, hand-cut strips of eggless dough.
fact: Rough-cut flour-and-water strips from Abruzzo, Molise and southern Lazio, classically simmered with beans. The uneven edges catch thick, brothy sauces in ways a clean-cut pasta cannot.

name: Tria
look: Short, irregular, eggless semolina ribbons.
fact: The name comes from Arabic itriya, a medieval word for dried pasta strands. In Salento's ciceri e tria, part of the pasta is fried crisp and stirred in with the boiled ribbons.

name: Dao xiao mian
look: Thick, uneven ribbons with a plump centre and thin, frilly edges.
fact: A Shanxi speciality. The cook holds a block of firm dough and shaves strips with a curved blade so that they fly directly into the boiling pot.

name: Erişte
look: Short, flat strips of egg noodle.
fact: The name comes from Persian reshteh. In Anatolian villages it is made in big batches at the end of summer, then dried and stored for winter.
